evidence.snippet:
# Microsoft eShopOnWeb ASP.NET Core Reference Application

This Microsoft reference application is now being maintained by [NimblePros](https://nimblepros.com/).

If you're looking for the .NET Aspire eShop sample it's [here](https://github.com/dotnet/eShop). Microsoft also recommends the [Reliable Web App](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/architecture/web-apps/guides/reliable-web-app/overview) patterns guidance for building web apps with enterprise app patterns.

Sample ASP.NET Core reference application, powered by Microsoft, demonstrating a single-process (monolithic) application architecture and deployment model. If you're new to .NET development, read the [Getting Started for Beginners](https://nimblepros.github.io/eShopOnWeb/getting-started-for-beginners.html) guide.

The **eShopOnWeb** sample is related to the [eShopOnContainers](https://github.com/dotnet/eShopOnContainers) sample application which, in that case, focuses on a microservices/containers-based application architecture. However, **eShopOnWeb** is much simpler in regards to its current functionality and focuses on traditional Web Application Development with a single deployment.

The goal for this sample is to demonstrate some of the principles and patterns described in the [eBook](https://aka.ms/webappebook). It is not meant to be an eCommerce reference application, and as such it does not implement many features that would be obvious and/or essential to a real eCommerce application.

The Azure Developer CLI (`azd`) is a developer-centric command-line interface (CLI) tool for creating Azure applications.

You need to install it before running and deploying with Azure Developer CLI.

### Windows

```powershell
powershell -ex AllSigned -c "Invoke-RestMethod 'https://aka.ms/install-azd.ps1' | Invoke-Expression"
```

### Linux/MacOS

```
curl -fsSL https://aka.ms/install-azd.sh | bash
```

And you can also install with package managers, like winget, choco, and brew. For more details, you can follow the documentation: https://aka.ms/azure-dev/install.

After logging in with the following command, you will be able to use the azd cli to quickly provision and deploy the application.

```
azd auth login
```

Then, execute the `azd init` command to initialize the environment.
```
azd init -t NimblePros/eShopOnWeb
```

Run `azd up` to provision all the resources to Azure and deploy the code to those resources.
```
azd up
```

### Configuring the sample to use SQL Server

1. By default, the project uses a real database. If you want an in memory database, you can add in the `appsettings.json` file in the Web folder

    ```json
   {
       "UseOnlyInMemoryDatabase": true
   }
    ```

1. Ensure your connection strings in `appsettings.json` point to a local SQL Server instance.
1. Ensure the tool EF was already installed. You can find some help [here](https://docs.microsoft.com/ef/core/miscellaneous/cli/dotnet)

    ```
    dotnet tool update --global dotnet-ef
    ```

1. Open a command prompt in the Web folder and execute the following commands:

    ```
    dotnet restore
    dotnet tool restore
    dotnet ef database update -c catalogcontext -p ../Infrastructure/Infrastructure.csproj -s Web.csproj
    dotnet ef database update -c appidentitydbcontext -p ../Infrastructure/Infrastructure.csproj -s Web.csproj
    ```

You can run the Web sample by running these commands from the root folder (where the .sln file is located):

```
docker-compose build
docker-compose up
```

narrative.executive_summary: The repository demonstrates strong testing practices with a high test coverage and meaningful assertions, supported by a clear modular structure and well-isolated data access layers. Authentication and authorization are implemented with vetted libraries and explicit route protections, though a critical issue exists where authentication middleware is not globally applied (AUTH-01@448c21f2be70). Security is weakened by the presence of a committed secret (SEC-01@448c21f2be70) and multiple vulnerable dependencies (SEC-02@448c21f2be70), alongside mutable GitHub action tags (SEC-03@448c21f2be70). Container and CI/CD configurations reveal several failures, including lack of non-root container user (CTR-01@448c21f2be70), missing health checks (CTR-05@448c21f2be70), and insufficient pipeline security practices (CI-03@448c21f2be70, CI-04@448c21f2be70, CI-05@448c21f2be70). Logging and documentation also show room for improvement, with sensitive data logged (LOG-04@448c21f2be70) and poor docstring coverage (DOC-04@448c21f2be70).

per_metric.text: Authentication is partially enforced; JWT authentication is registered but not globally applied due to missing middleware (AUTH-01@448c21f2be70). Authorization is properly configured with role checks protecting privileged operations (AUTH-03@448c21f2be70), and unauthenticated routes are explicitly declared (AUTH-02@448c21f2be70). Passwords are securely hashed using ASP.NET Core Identity (AUTH-05@448c21f2be70).

The CI pipeline exists with multiple workflows and runs build and tests, but lacks a lint step (CI-02@448c21f2be70). Several failures include actionlint errors (CI-03@448c21f2be70), workflows using default or overly permissive token permissions (CI-04@448c21f2be70), and third-party actions not pinned to commit SHAs (CI-05@448c21f2be70).

Container configurations use pinned base images and multi-stage builds with a .dockerignore file present (CTR-02@448c21f2be70, CTR-03@448c21f2be70, CTR-04@448c21f2be70). However, containers run as root (CTR-01@448c21f2be70), lack health checks or probes (CTR-05@448c21f2be70), and infrastructure code has multiple misconfigurations flagged by checkov (CTR-06@448c21f2be70). Dockerfiles are free of hadolint errors (CTR-07@448c21f2be70).

Data access is well isolated behind repository layers (DATA-03@448c21f2be70) and schema changes are managed by migrations (DATA-01@448c21f2be70). Connection settings are mostly from configuration or secret stores, but Docker appsettings contain hard-coded credentials (DATA-02@448c21f2be70). Multi-step writes are implemented without explicit transaction wrapping (DATA-04@448c21f2be70).

The README provides purpose, setup, and run instructions (DOC-01@448c21f2be70), and architecture decisions are documented (DOC-03@448c21f2be70). A contributing guide is present (DOC-05@448c21f2be70). However, no API documentation is generated (DOC-02@448c21f2be70), and docstring coverage for public functions is very low at four percent (DOC-04@448c21f2be70).

Logging includes request correlation and trace context propagation (LOG-03@448c21f2be70), but print/console output is still present in production code (LOG-02@448c21f2be70). Sensitive data such as email recipients and message bodies are logged, exposing personal information (LOG-04@448c21f2be70). No telemetry SDK or health endpoints are configured (LOG-05@448c21f2be70).

Performance is generally good with non-blocking IO in request paths (PERF-01@448c21f2be70), no N+1 query patterns (PERF-02@448c21f2be70), caching for expensive reads (PERF-03@448c21f2be70), and paginated list endpoints (PERF-04@448c21f2be70). However, outbound HTTP calls lack timeouts and retries (PERF-05@448c21f2be70), and resource limits are not configured for deployments (PERF-06@448c21f2be70).

Security is weakened by a committed secret in the repository (SEC-01@448c21f2be70) and multiple dependencies with critical or high vulnerabilities (SEC-02@448c21f2be70). Static analysis finds high-severity issues related to mutable GitHub action tags (SEC-03@448c21f2be70). On the positive side, database queries are parameterized (SEC-05@448c21f2be70), CORS and security headers are safely configured (SEC-06@448c21f2be70), and automated dependency updates are configured (SEC-07@448c21f2be70).

The codebase has clear module and layer boundaries with controllers delegating to handlers and repositories (STR-01@448c21f2be70). No oversized source files or overly complex functions were found (STR-02@448c21f2be70, STR-03@448c21f2be70). Configuration is properly separated from code (STR-05@448c21f2be70). However, most dependency manifests lack lockfiles and have unpinned dependencies (STR-06@448c21f2be70).

Testing is a strong area with a comprehensive test suite of fifty files and over one hundred tests (TEST-01@448c21f2be70). Tests are proportionate to source code size (TEST-02@448c21f2be70), executed in CI (TEST-03@448c21f2be70), and coverage is measured (TEST-04@448c21f2be70). Tests contain meaningful assertions verifying repository calls and outcomes (TEST-05@448c21f2be70).
